blocks.content: Six topics have built a complete case for Ingress. That case was never that LoadBalancer is wrong. It is that Ingress is the better tool for a specific, common shape of problem. This final topic draws that line precisely.
Ingress vs LoadBalancer, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: Ingress vs LoadBalancer, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: LoadBalancer, covered in full in the previous module, provisions a dedicated external cloud load balancer directly in front of a single Service, giving that one Service a genuine, stable, external entry point with no HTTP awareness involved at all.

Ingress, covered across every topic in this module, provisions one shared external entry point in front of an Ingress controller, which then applies HTTP aware routing rules to direct traffic across potentially many different backend Services.

Neither approach is universally correct. Each solves a genuinely different shape of problem, and choosing between them deliberately, rather than defaulting to whichever was learned first, is the practical skill this closing topic is built to give.

This topic assumes full familiarity with everything covered about LoadBalancer in the previous module and everything covered about Ingress across the six topics preceding this one, and focuses entirely on the direct comparison between the two.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643105460-171641616.png
blocks.alt: Ingress vs LoadBalancer given its own full depth

blocks.content: A Direct Side by Side Comparison
blocks.text: A Direct Side by Side Comparison

blocks.content: LoadBalancer works at Layer 4, has no awareness of HTTP, and provisions one dedicated external address per Service. Ingress works at Layer 7, is fully HTTP aware, and provisions one shared external address for potentially many Services.

LoadBalancer supports any TCP or UDP protocol, including non HTTP traffic such as raw database connections or custom binary protocols. Ingress is fundamentally scoped to HTTP and HTTPS traffic specifically, and cannot route non HTTP protocols at all.

LoadBalancer's cost scales linearly with the number of exposed Services, one billed load balancer per Service. Ingress's cost stays flat as more HTTP applications are added, since they all share the exact same controller and the exact same load balancer in front of it.

Neither list of tradeoffs makes one option strictly better. They describe two tools built for two different jobs, and the right choice depends entirely on the specific shape of the traffic and the application being exposed.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643107091-233840605.png
blocks.alt: A side by side comparison of both approaches

A Real Comparison at Twenty Microservices
blocks.text: A Real Comparison at Twenty Microservices

blocks.content: Consider a cluster running twenty HTTP based microservices, each needing genuine external reachability, directly the scenario this entire module has been building toward addressing since its very first topic.

Using LoadBalancer for all twenty means provisioning twenty separate cloud load balancers, twenty separate billed resources, and twenty separate external addresses that DNS and any client integration would need to individually track and manage.

Using Ingress for all twenty means provisioning exactly one cloud load balancer in front of one Ingress controller, with twenty host or path based rules directing traffic to the correct backend, exactly the pattern demonstrated throughout this module's real examples.

The cost difference alone, one billed load balancer instead of twenty, is often decisive on its own, before even considering the added operational simplicity of managing one set of Ingress rules instead of twenty separately provisioned external addresses.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643108746-290293259.png
blocks.alt: Twenty microservices behind one Ingress instead of twenty load balancers

blocks.content: Recap: The Mistake This Entire Module Answers
blocks.text: Recap: The Mistake This Entire Module Answers

blocks.content: The LoadBalancer topic in the previous module explicitly warned against provisioning one LoadBalancer Service per application component, describing exactly the twenty microservice, twenty load balancer scenario just walked through in the previous section.

That warning promised Ingress as the more cost effective, more manageable solution for exactly this shape of problem, and every single topic in this module since has been building the complete, practical case for exactly that promise.

Reading this comparison topic as the fulfillment of that specific promise, rather than as a neutral, abstract comparison between two equally weighted options, is the correct way to understand why this module exists immediately after the one that raised the original concern.

This does not mean LoadBalancer was ever the wrong choice categorically. It means LoadBalancer applied indiscriminately, to every single Service regardless of its actual traffic shape, was the specific mistake this module has spent seven topics correcting.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643110335-498087651.png
blocks.alt: Recap of the one load balancer per Service mistake, already covered

blocks.content: A Practical Decision Framework

If the traffic is HTTP or HTTPS, and especially if there are multiple applications that could reasonably share one entry point, Ingress is almost always the better fit, delivering lower cost and centralized, declarative routing management.

If the traffic is not HTTP, such as a raw database protocol, a custom TCP based service, or anything requiring UDP, Ingress simply cannot help, since it is fundamentally scoped to HTTP aware routing, and LoadBalancer remains the correct and only real choice.

If an application, even an HTTP based one, has a genuine, specific need for complete network isolation from every other application, its own entirely dedicated LoadBalancer may still be the more appropriate choice despite the added cost.

This decision framework, applied deliberately to every new externally facing component rather than defaulting reflexively to whichever mechanism was used most recently, is the single most valuable practical skill this entire module has been building toward.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643112035-288356123.png

A Common Mistake: Ingress for Non HTTP Workloads
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: Ingress for Non HTTP Workloads

blocks.content: A common mistake, made specifically by teams who have internalized this module's lessons a little too literally, is attempting to route a non HTTP workload, such as a raw PostgreSQL connection or a custom TCP protocol, through an Ingress object.

Ingress simply has no mechanism for this. Its entire routing model is built around HTTP concepts, host headers and URL paths, neither of which exists in a raw TCP or UDP connection carrying a non HTTP protocol.

Some Ingress controller implementations offer a limited, controller specific extension for basic TCP or UDP stream passthrough, but this is a special case addon, not core Ingress functionality, and should not be relied upon as a general substitute for LoadBalancer.

The correct response to a genuine non HTTP external exposure need is simply using LoadBalancer directly, exactly as covered in the previous module, rather than forcing an HTTP focused tool into a job it was never designed to do.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643113677-178950203.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of using Ingress for a non HTTP TCP or UDP workload

blocks.content: Cost Modeling the Two Approaches Concretely
blocks.text: Cost Modeling the Two Approaches Concretely

blocks.content: Modeling real cost concretely makes the decision easier to justify beyond intuition alone: twenty LoadBalancer Services, each billed hourly by a cloud provider, sum to a meaningfully larger recurring cost than one shared load balancer fronting an Ingress controller.

This cost gap widens further as an organization grows, since every additional HTTP based microservice under the LoadBalancer approach adds another full, separately billed load balancer, while the same addition under Ingress adds only one more inexpensive routing rule.

Building a simple cost model, even a rough one, comparing the two approaches at an organization's current and projected future microservice count, is a genuinely persuasive, concrete way to justify Ingress adoption to stakeholders focused primarily on infrastructure cost.

This concrete cost framing is often more effective at driving real adoption than the architectural or operational arguments alone, since it translates directly into a number that resonates clearly with anyone responsible for cloud infrastructure spending.
Operational Complexity as a Second Dimension
blocks.text: Operational Complexity as a Second Dimension

blocks.content: Beyond raw cost, operational complexity is a second, equally important dimension worth weighing: twenty separately provisioned LoadBalancer Services also mean twenty separate external addresses to track, twenty separate DNS records, and twenty separate points of potential misconfiguration.

Ingress consolidates this operational surface area dramatically, centralizing routing configuration into a small number of Ingress manifests, reviewable, version controlled, and reasoned about as a cohesive whole rather than twenty scattered, independent pieces of infrastructure.

This reduced operational surface area directly reduces the likelihood of a specific class of mistake: a forgotten, orphaned LoadBalancer Service left running long after its application was decommissioned, quietly accumulating cost with no one aware it still exists.

Weighing both cost and operational complexity together, rather than focusing on cost alone, gives a genuinely complete picture of why Ingress tends to be the correct default for the majority of a typical organization's HTTP based workloads.
Team Ownership Models Under Each Approach
blocks.text: Team Ownership Models Under Each Approach

blocks.content: Under a pure LoadBalancer approach, each team owning an application also directly owns its own external exposure, with no shared infrastructure or shared configuration to coordinate with any other team across the organization.

Under an Ingress approach, teams typically share a common Ingress controller, owned and operated by a platform or infrastructure team, while individual application teams own only their own specific Ingress rules within that shared infrastructure.

This shared ownership model requires a small amount of upfront organizational coordination, deciding who owns the controller itself versus who owns individual rules, but it scales considerably better than fully independent, uncoordinated LoadBalancer ownership as an organization grows.

Establishing this ownership model clearly and early, rather than leaving it ambiguous, prevents a common source of friction where no team feels responsible for the shared Ingress controller's own health, resource sizing, or version upgrades.
Revisiting the Decision as Applications Evolve
blocks.text: Revisiting the Decision as Applications Evolve

blocks.content: The Ingress versus LoadBalancer decision is not necessarily permanent for any given application. A component that started behind Ingress may later develop a genuine need for dedicated network isolation, warranting a migration to its own LoadBalancer Service.

Conversely, a component that started with its own dedicated LoadBalancer, perhaps provisioned early before an Ingress controller was even installed on the cluster, is very often a strong candidate for later consolidation behind the shared Ingress controller once one exists.

Treating this as a decision worth periodically revisiting, rather than a one time choice made permanently at an application's initial deployment, keeps a cluster's overall external exposure architecture aligned with its actual, current needs rather than its historical ones.

This periodic revisiting is a natural extension of the best practices already covered earlier in this topic, and it closes the loop on treating this decision as a genuinely deliberate, ongoing architectural choice rather than a single, static, one time judgment.
Using Both Together in the Same Cluster
blocks.text: Using Both Together in the Same Cluster

blocks.content: Most real production clusters use both mechanisms simultaneously, not as a contradiction, but as the correct application of each tool to the specific part of the system it fits best.

The bulk of HTTP based microservices and web applications route through a single Ingress controller, while a small number of genuinely non HTTP workloads, such as a message queue or a database needing direct external access, each retain their own dedicated LoadBalancer Service.

This combined approach captures the cost and manageability benefits of Ingress for the majority of typical traffic, while preserving LoadBalancer's full protocol flexibility for the specific minority of cases that genuinely require it.

Recognizing that the choice is not exclusive, and that a well designed cluster often uses both deliberately and simultaneously, is a more mature and more practically useful understanding than treating the decision as a single, cluster wide, either or choice.
Migration Considerations Between the Two

Migrating an existing LoadBalancer Service to Ingress typically involves installing an Ingress controller if one is not already present, creating an Ingress object with a rule pointing at the existing Service, and then updating DNS to point at the Ingress controller's address instead.

This migration can typically be performed gradually, one application at a time, since Ingress and LoadBalancer Services can coexist on the same cluster throughout the transition without any conflict between them.

A brief period of running both the old LoadBalancer and the new Ingress route side by side, before finally cutting DNS over and decommissioning the old LoadBalancer, is a genuinely safe, low risk way to validate the new routing path before fully committing to it.

This gradual, coexistence friendly migration path is one more reason Ingress adoption tends to spread naturally through an organization over time, rather than requiring a single, risky, all at once cutover across every application simultaneously.
Best Practices for Choosing Between Them
blocks.text: Best Practices for Choosing Between Them

blocks.content: Default new HTTP based applications to Ingress from the very beginning, treating it as the standard, expected pattern for web facing traffic rather than something adopted only after a LoadBalancer cost problem is already noticed.

Reserve LoadBalancer deliberately for genuinely non HTTP workloads, or for the specific, well justified cases where an HTTP application genuinely needs complete, dedicated network isolation from everything else in the cluster.

Revisit this decision periodically as an application's actual needs evolve, since a component that started with a genuine isolation requirement may later be a perfectly reasonable candidate for consolidation behind the shared Ingress controller.

Document the reasoning behind any LoadBalancer Service used for an HTTP application specifically, since a future engineer reviewing the manifest will otherwise reasonably assume it should have used Ingress by default, exactly as this module recommends.

blocks.content: The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

Ingress and LoadBalancer are not competitors. They are two tools solving two genuinely different problems, and the entire value of this module lies in knowing precisely which problem is actually in front of you before reaching for either one.

For the overwhelming majority of modern, HTTP based applications, especially in any cluster running more than a small handful of externally facing components, Ingress is the correct default, delivering lower cost and centralized, declarative routing.

LoadBalancer remains fully correct and fully necessary for genuinely non HTTP traffic, and understanding both mechanisms in full depth, exactly as this course now has across two complete modules, is what makes this decision a deliberate, informed one rather than a coin flip.
This closes Module Seven in its entirety. The next module, Configuration, shifts focus from how traffic reaches an application to how that application is actually configured once traffic arrives.

One final, practical reminder before moving on: a cost model, however rough, is often the most persuasive argument for consolidating behind Ingress, so keep one handy when making this case to a team weighing infrastructure spend.

blocks.title: Ingress vs LoadBalancer In Full
points: LoadBalancer operates at Layer 4 with full protocol flexibility and one dedicated external address per Service; Ingress operates at Layer 7, HTTP and HTTPS only, with one shared address for many Services.
Ingress directly answers the one load balancer per Service cost problem raised at the end of the previous module, for the specific case of HTTP based traffic.
The practical decision framework is straightforward: HTTP traffic with multiple applications favors Ingress; non HTTP protocols or genuine isolation needs favor LoadBalancer.
Most real production clusters use both simultaneously, applying each tool deliberately to the specific part of the system it fits best, rather than treating the choice as exclusive.

This closes Module Seven (Ingress) in full. Module Eight, Configuration, covers how applications are configured once traffic, routed by everything covered across these last two modules, actually arrives.
